newsitem.title: ITALY: Exiled Italian royal welcomes moves for his return.
newsitem.headline: Exiled Italian royal welcomes moves for his return.

text.p: The exiled son of Italy's last king welcomed on Thursday moves to allow him to come home 50 years after the monarchy was abolished but insisted he would not renounce his royal prerogatives.

"I believe this is a step in the right direction towards a solution to a problem which is painful for me but shameful for a civilized society," Italian newspapers quoted Vittorio Emanuele as saying from his home in Switzerland.

"I was hit by shock," he said, referring to the Italian government's backing on Wednesday for a proposed draft law to allow him to come home for the first time since all male heirs of the royal family were barred entry in 1946.
But Vittorio Emanuele told the daily La Repubblica newspaper that he would not renounce his royal claims.
"No one with sense can ask someone to renounce their family, their traditions or their duty to keep these intact and transmit them to their heirs," he said.
Vittorio Emanuele was forced into exile with his father Umberto II when he was nine years old.
War-weary Italians had voted to scrap the monarchy on June 2, 1946, blaming the royal family for complicity in the fascist dictatorship of Benito Mussolini.
Umberto II died in exile in 1983, leaving Vittorio Emanuele as next in line to the Italian throne.

He may be allowed to return to Italy from his present home in Geneva if the draft, which will be drawn up at a future cabinet meeting, is passed by both houses of parliament, allowing it to become law.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told reporters on Thursday that the legal process could be lengthy.

"The government at yesterday's cabinet meeting approved the idea of a draft constitutional law being presented, which undoubtedly requires a very long passage because it needs to go through several parliamentary stages," he said.
"It is therefore not an immediate thing."
Vittorio Emmanuele told Rome daily Il Messaggero that despite his claims to the throne he did not intend to get involved in Italian politics if he returned.
"I would not dream of mixing myself up in electoral campaigns. I would like to help the development of my country, whose laws I will respect," he said.
Many Italians, including President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and his predecessors as head of state, have called on the country to forget the past and change the 1946 law.

The hard-right National Alliance and the Monarchist Party welcomed Wednesday's move amid criticism that the government was pandering to right-wing voters. Italian deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni denied these suggestions.
But the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which secures Prodi's parliamentary majority, said the Savoy dynasty could not be so easily forgiven for its role in the country's fascist past.
"As long as the dynasty remains, there also remains their gigantic responsibility for the fascist regime," Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti told reporters on Wednesday.

The House of Savoy united Italy when Vittorio Emanuele I of Piedmont became the country's first king in 1861. The former royal palace atop the Quirinale hill in Rome is now the president's official residence.
